---
title: "Testing the wind disruption hypothesis for beetle refugia"
subtitle: "Host distribution, thermal load, and terrain-wind effects on Mountain pine beetle attack (Dendroctonus ponderosae) across 1,740 m of relief in the Selkirk Mountains of British Columbia"
author:
  - name: Seamus Murphy
    orcid: 0000-0002-1792-0351
    email: seamusrobertmurphy@gmail.com
abstract: >
  Refugia from mountain pine beetle (Dendroctonus ponderosae) are hypothesised to form where host is sparse enough
  for wind to disrupt the aggregation pheromone plume mass attack depends on, never tested spatially.
  We test it across 168 km² of inventoried forest and 1,740 m of relief in British Columbia, combining an aerial
  survey of beetle-caused mortality (1999-2015) with inventory host cover and Global Wind Atlas speed. Attack is
  unimodal, peaking near 1,430 m. Below 1,900 m that peak is host, and conditioning on lodgepole presence removes
  it; above 1,900 m it is not, and attack halves while pine cover thins only slightly. We find no wind effect.
  Orthogonalised against a linear elevation term, wind is the strongest negative predictor in host-bearing stands,
  clearing the interval test at every severity threshold above trace; but a unimodal response leaves elevation's
  curvature inside that term, and refitting it as a quadratic or spline collapses the coefficient everywhere. The
  signal is a specification artefact. Winter minima at every station within 100 km fall ten degrees short of lethal,
  so the cold mechanism is degree-day accumulation, not freeze. Elevation explains 0.63 of the wind
  surface's variance landscape-wide but 0.80 within a 2 by 4 km clip, where the estimate reverses sign; grain
  scarcely matters. At the extent disturbance ecology usually adopts, this study would have reported the
  opposite; with severity collapsed to presence, no result at all; and without a host layer, absence of pine
  misread as refugia.

```{r}
                plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10)))

B_BOOT   <- 150L    # spatial block bootstrap replicates
BLOCK    <- 40L     # block side in cells (40 x 25.1 m ~= 1 km)
OUTBREAK <- 1999:2015
## The elevation above which conditioning on host stops removing the decline.
## It is a band edge of the 200 m banding in @tbl-gradient and is quoted in the
## prose, so it is defined once here rather than typed into each comparison.
ALPINE   <- 1900
```

```{r}
#| label: map-furniture
#| echo: false

## Cartography shared by the four map figures, defined once here so each figure can
## sit in the section it documents instead of being grouped at the end of Materials
## for want of its furniture. Graticule, EPSG, north arrow, bar scale and a
## representative fraction quoted against a stated printed width are set once and
## reused, so the panels are directly comparable.

clip_src <- rast(dpath("beetle_stages", "Beetle.Oubteak.2005.tif"))
clip_sf  <- st_as_sf(project(as.polygons(ext(clip_src), crs = crs(clip_src)), crs(G)))
grid_sf  <- st_as_sf(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)))
ev <- as.vector(ext(G)); gw <- ev["xmax"] - ev["xmin"]; gh <- ev["ymax"] - ev["ymin"]
sub_utm <- "EPSG:32611 WGS 84 / UTM 11N"

map_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = .25, linetype = "dotted"),
        axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text = element_text(size = 6, colour = "grey25"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 8.5, margin = margin(b = 1)),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 6, colour = "grey35", margin = margin(b = 3)),
        legend.key.width = unit(3.2, "mm"), legend.key.height = unit(7, "mm"),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 6.5), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))

north <- annotation_north_arrow(location = "tr", which_north = "true",
  height = unit(6, "mm"), width = unit(5, "mm"),
  pad_x = unit(1.2, "mm"), pad_y = unit(1.2, "mm"),
  style = north_arrow_orienteering(text_size = 5, line_width = .6,
    fill = c("white", "grey20"), text_col = "grey20"))

## White plates behind the north arrow and the clip label. Without them the arrow is
## unreadable over the dark end of the wind ramp and the label collides with the
## severity polygons.
plate <- annotate("rect", xmin = ev["xmin"] + .885*gw, xmax = ev["xmax"],
                  ymin = ev["ymax"] - .115*gh, ymax = ev["ymax"],
                  fill = "white", alpha = .72, colour = NA)
clip_layer <- geom_sf(data = clip_sf, fill = NA, colour = "#C0392B", linewidth = .45)
study <- list(coord_sf(crs = 32611, datum = st_crs(4326), expand = FALSE,
                       xlim = ev[c("xmin","xmax")], ylim = ev[c("ymin","ymax")]),
              scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-116.75, -116.60, .05)),
              scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(49.10, 49.24, .05)),
              plate, north, map_theme)

## Colour limits from robust quantiles. The raw topographic position surface runs
## past 1,000 m at the grid edge, where the 625 m window is truncated, and on a
## full-range ramp that artefact flattens the whole interior to one colour.
panel <- function(r, title, legend, pal = "viridis", dir = 1, q = c(.02, .98)) {
  lim <- unname(quantile(values(r, mat = FALSE), q, na.rm = TRUE))
  ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = r) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = pal, direction = dir, na.value = "grey88",
                         name = legend, limits = lim, oob = scales::squish) +
    clip_layer + study + labs(title = title, subtitle = sub_utm)
}
```

# Introduction

Disturbance refugia, defined by @krawchuk2020 as locations disturbed less severely or less frequently than the surrounding landscape, have become an organising concept for forest conservation under climate change. The concept is well developed for fire and much less so for insects. @krawchuk2020 note that few studies have explicitly identified refugia from insect outbreaks, and propose a testable mechanism for the most consequential insect disturbance in western North America: refugia from mountain pine beetle (*Dendroctonus ponderosae* Hopkins) could occur where host density is lower, thinner stands admitting more wind and so disrupting the aggregation pheromone communication mass attack depends on.

The hypothesis is attractive because it is mechanistic and because each of its parts is independently plausible. Mass attack requires beetles to overwhelm host defences in a coordinated pulse, and the coordination is chemical. Beetle dispersal above the canopy is a flight behaviour sensitive to ambient conditions [@gray1972; @jones2019]. Thinner stands admit more wind. What has been missing is a spatial test.

@cartwright2018 came closest. Working at 30 m in lodgepole and whitebark pine in southern Oregon, she identified refugia from Landsat moisture anomalies during a 2009 drought and beetle outbreak and modelled their landscape controls. Refugia were associated with shaded slopes, convergent positions, low soil bulk density and thinner stands. The thinner-stand result is the host-density half of the hypothesis, confirmed. But she had no wind surface, so the mechanism went untested.

Testing it requires a wind surface, and that is where the problem starts. Gridded wind products, the Global Wind Atlas among them, are produced by downscaling coarse mesoscale fields over a digital elevation model [@davis2023; @badger2014]. A surface built this way is in part a transform of the terrain it was draped over. Offered to a model alongside elevation it is not an independent measurement, and the severity of the dependence is a function of extent: a coarse driving field is nearly flat over a few kilometres, so at small extents almost all the variation in the product is terrain. An analyst working at the scale of a burn perimeter or a cluster of field plots, which is where most disturbance ecology is done, is in the worst position and has the least warning.

A second and more elementary trap attends refugia work. A cell that was not attacked may hold no host. Under the @krawchuk2020 framing this is the difference between what a place is a refugium *from* and what it is a refugium *for*, and it cannot be resolved without an independent map of host abundance. The precedent is old and pointed: @hadley1994 predicted heavier beetle mortality on hot, dry, south-facing slopes and found the reverse, because host density rather than moisture stress governed where attack succeeded.

We take these three problems to one landscape. We ask:

1.  Does terrain condition beetle-caused mortality once host abundance is accounted for, and where along the elevation gradient does host stop explaining the pattern?
2.  Does the component of the wind surface that is independent of elevation predict reduced attack where host is present, as @krawchuk2020 hypothesise?
3.  How much does the answer to question 2 depend on decisions the analyst makes freely: the extent of the study area, the grain of the cells, and whether damage is coded as a binary or as the ordinal severity class the survey records?

The design makes the third question answerable rather than rhetorical. The same response, predictors and model are refitted across each axis: across the full landscape and inside a 2 by 4 km clip drawn from it, at 25 m, 50 m and 100 m, and at each severity threshold in turn. Two of the three change the answer, and they are not the two that get reported.

# Materials

## Study area

The Darkwoods Conservation Area lies in the South Selkirk Mountains of southeastern British Columbia. The terrain grid spans 16 by 17.5 km and `r format(round(GRID_RELIEF), big.mark = ",")` m of relief, from valley bottom to alpine. The modelled area is a subset, because cells carrying no inventory basal area cannot enter a model conditioning on stand structure; @tbl-relief reports its extent and relief. Both numbers are correct and are not interchangeable. The range crosses the full biogeoclimatic sequence of the southern interior wet belt, from the dry warm Interior Cedar-Hemlock subzones through the moist warm subzones to the Engelmann Spruce-Subalpine Fir zone and its parkland variant [@ketcheson1991; @braumandl2005]. Lodgepole pine (*Pinus contorta* var. *latifolia*), the beetle's principal host here, occupies the middle of that sequence and is scarce at both ends.

The site description and terrain surfaces are inherited from a companion analysis of conifer regeneration on the same ground [@murphy2026], which used them to predict seedling intensity after a 2015 wildfire. Disturbance was a predictor there; here it is the response. @fig-site locates the landscape and shows the three spatial inputs.

## Beetle-caused mortality

```{r}
#| label: read-response
#| echo: false

aos_box <- ext(project(as.polygons(ext(G), crs = crs(G)), "EPSG:3005"))
aos <- vect(here("02.inputs/aos/pest_infestation_poly.gdb"),
            layer = "pest_infestation_poly", extent = aos_box)
mpb <- project(aos[aos$PEST_SPECIES_CODE == "IBM", ], crs(G))   # IBM = mountain pine beetle
m   <- mpb[mpb$CAPTURE_YEAR %in% OUTBREAK, ]

## BC severity classes are ordinal: trace, light, moderate, severe, very severe
sev_rank <- c(T = 1, L = 2, M = 3, S = 4, V = 5)
m$sev <- unname(sev_rank[m$PEST_SEVERITY_CODE]); m$sev[is.na(m$sev)] <- 0

severity  <- rasterize(m, G, field = "sev", fun = "max", background = 0)

c(polygons = nrow(m), years = length(unique(m$CAPTURE_YEAR)),
  hectares = round(sum(m$AREA_HA)))
```

The response is the British Columbia Aerial Overview Survey, the operational provincial record of forest health, in which observers sketch-map damage annually from aircraft and label each polygon by year, causal agent, severity class and host species. We take polygons coded `IBM`, mountain pine beetle, for the outbreak window 1999 to 2015, and rasterise the maximum severity class reached by each cell.

Using the survey rather than a spectral classification is a deliberate trade. Red attack has been mapped from Landsat with improving accuracy [@white2005; @meddens2013; @ye2021], but every such product is a model whose errors are spatially structured and not independent of terrain, because illumination, shadow and view angle vary with slope and aspect. For a question about terrain, a response from a terrain-sensitive classifier risks recovering the classifier's own terrain sensitivity. Sketch-mapping has cruder errors, but they are observer errors, not errors generated by the predictors under test.

The severity scale is anchored to ground measurement. Twenty-eight field plots established in beetle-affected stands in 2020 recorded the basal area of pine killed, spanning 0.6 to 47.4 m2/ha, or 1.3 to 94.7 per cent of plot basal area, and calibrated the spectral mapping used in the companion study [@murphy2026]. Plot coordinates were not recoverable, so the plots calibrate the severity scale but cannot check the spatial placement of individual polygons. We state that limit rather than implying a validation we did not perform.

@fig-site shows the landscape and the response together. Panel (b) is the elevation surface that defines the grid and panel (d) the survey record this paper models: attack concentrated in a mid-elevation band, sparse in the valley and again along the alpine crest. Panel (c) is the wind surface whose relationship to that terrain the second half of the paper is about.

```{r}
#| label: fig-site
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.1
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| fig-cap: "The study area and the three spatial inputs. (a) Location within British Columbia; the marker is a 22 km symbol, not the footprint. (b) The elevation surface, which is the analysis grid. (c) Global Wind Atlas mean speed at 10 m; the shaded southern band lies outside the wind product's extent. (d) Beetle-caused mortality from the Aerial Overview Survey, 1999 to 2015, as the maximum severity class in any year. The outlined rectangle in (b) to (d) is the 2 by 4 km clip of @sec-extent. Graticules are WGS 84; each panel's projection is beneath its title."

## The wind raster begins 715 m north of the grid's southern edge, so resampling onto G
## turns that strip into NA cells and na.value draws it grey. Left transparent it reads
## as a rendering fault rather than as missing data.
Wind_r <- resample(rast(dpath("terrain_environment", "Wind.utm.tif")), G)

prov <- st_transform(ne_states(country = c("Canada","United States of America"),
                               returnclass = "sf"), 3005)
site <- st_transform(st_centroid(grid_sf), 3005)
lab  <- transform(as.data.frame(st_coordinates(site)), lab = "Darkwoods\nstudy area")
## BC is framed to the analysis grid's aspect ratio so the two rows of the figure are
## the same height and no band of white opens between them.
b0 <- st_bbox(prov[prov$name == "British Columbia", ]); tgt <- unname(gw/gh)
w0 <- unname(b0["xmax"]-b0["xmin"]); h0 <- unname(b0["ymax"]-b0["ymin"])
cx <- unname(b0["xmax"]+b0["xmin"])/2; cy <- unname(b0["ymax"]+b0["ymin"])/2
if (w0/h0 > tgt) h0 <- w0/tgt else w0 <- h0*tgt
pd <- .04*w0
bb <- c(xmin = cx-w0/2-pd, xmax = cx+w0/2+pd, ymin = cy-h0/2-pd, ymax = cy+h0/2+pd)

p_a <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = prov[prov$name != "British Columbia", ], fill = "grey93",
          colour = "grey65", linewidth = .2) +
  geom_sf(data = prov[prov$name == "British Columbia", ], fill = "grey82",
          colour = "grey30", linewidth = .4) +
  geom_sf(data = st_buffer(site, 22000), fill = "#C0392B", colour = "grey15",
          linewidth = .3) +
  geom_label_repel(data = lab, aes(X, Y, label = lab), size = 2.1, lineheight = .95,
                   colour = "grey10", nudge_x = -330000, nudge_y = 300000,
                   segment.colour = "grey25", segment.size = .3, min.segment.length = 0,
                   box.padding = .4, seed = 1, fill = "white", alpha = .9,
                   label.size = 0, label.padding = unit(.7, "mm")) +
  annotate("text", x = bb["xmin"] + .34*(bb["xmax"]-bb["xmin"]),
           y = bb["ymin"] + .70*(bb["ymax"]-bb["ymin"]), label = "British\nColumbia",
           size = 2.3, colour = "grey30", fontface = "italic", lineheight = .95) +
  coord_sf(crs = 3005, xlim = bb[c("xmin","xmax")], ylim = bb[c("ymin","ymax")],
           datum = st_crs(4326), expand = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-135, -115, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(48, 60, 3)) +
  north + map_theme +
  labs(title = "(a) Location", subtitle = "EPSG:3005 NAD83 / BC Albers")

p_b <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = G) +
  scale_fill_hypso_c(palette = "dem_screen", na.value = "transparent",
                     name = "Elevation\n(m)") +
  clip_layer + study + labs(title = "(b) Elevation, the analysis grid", subtitle = sub_utm)

p_c <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = Wind_r) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, na.value = "grey88",
                       name = "Wind speed\n(m s⁻¹)") +
  clip_layer + study +
  labs(title = "(c) Global Wind Atlas mean speed at 10 m", subtitle = sub_utm)

sev_f <- as.factor(severity)
levels(sev_f) <- data.frame(ID = 0:5, class = c("none","trace","light","moderate",
                                                "severe","very severe"))
p_d <- ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = sev_f) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(none = "grey92", trace = "#FEE0B6", light = "#FDB863",
                    moderate = "#E08214", severe = "#B35806", `very severe` = "#7F3B08"),
                    na.value = "transparent", name = "Severity\nclass",
                    na.translate = FALSE) +
  clip_layer + study +
  labs(title = "(d) Beetle-caused mortality, 1999 to 2015", subtitle = sub_utm)

fig_site <- (p_a | p_b) / (p_c | p_d)
fig_site
ggsave("../03.outputs/PNG/fig-site-maps.png", fig_site,
```
